prompt: How many copies of each 10 GB segment does Aurora keep, and where?

choices.text: Two, one in each of two zones, like Multi-AZ
choices.why: That is the RDS Multi-AZ instance; Aurora writes each segment six times.

choices.text: Six: two in each of three zones
choices.why: Right. The six copies of one segment are a protection group.

choices.text: Three, one per zone, with a read quorum of two
choices.why: There are two copies per zone, six in all; the read quorum is three of six.

choices.text: One per instance in the cluster
choices.why: Instances share one volume; the number of copies has nothing to do with them.

prompt: Zone `sa-east-1c` goes dark, taking two of a protection group's six copies. What can the cluster still do?

choices.text: Read, but not write, until the zone comes back
choices.why: Four copies are left, which is exactly the write quorum.

choices.text: Nothing, until a failover moves the volume
choices.why: The volume is not moved; it is still spread across the other two zones.

choices.text: Write only to the copies in `sa-east-1a`
choices.why: Writes go to every copy that answers, and four answering is enough.

choices.text: Both read and write, with four copies left
choices.why: Right. A zone is the failure Aurora is designed to survive without stopping writes.

prompt: Why does Aurora pick a write quorum of 4 and a read quorum of 3 out of 6, rather than 3 and 3?
hint: Add the two numbers and compare with six.

choices.text: 3 and 3 would be faster, and 4 and 3 is a compromise on price
choices.why: Price is not the reason; with 3 and 3 a read could miss the latest write.

choices.text: With 4 + 3 above 6, a read always meets a copy that has the latest write
choices.why: Right. Two sets of 3 could be disjoint; 4 and 3 cannot.

choices.text: Writes need one extra copy for the replica's cache
choices.why: Replicas read the storage like anyone else; the quorum is about overlap.

choices.text: Three zones need an odd number of copies per zone
choices.why: There are two per zone, an even number; the reason is the overlap.

prompt: What does an Aurora writer send to the storage layer when a transaction commits?

choices.text: The changed data pages, to six copies
choices.why: That is how an RDS instance and its mirror work; Aurora sends no pages.

choices.text: Log records only, which the storage nodes apply to the pages
choices.why: Right. Which makes a commit a small network write, and lets replicas share the volume.

choices.text: A snapshot of the volume, every five minutes
choices.why: That confuses the commit with the backups of lesson 7.

choices.text: The whole transaction to each replica, which writes it to disk
choices.why: Replicas have no disk of their own; they read the shared volume.

prompt: Quitanda creates an Aurora cluster and then two instances in it. Which one is the writer?
hint: A cluster has exactly one writer.

choices.text: The one with the larger instance class
choices.why: Size breaks a tie between replicas at failover; it does not choose the first writer.

choices.text: Both, one per zone
choices.why: Aurora has one writer per cluster; the other instance is a replica.

choices.text: The first one created
choices.why: Right. Every instance after it is a replica, until a failover moves the role.

choices.text: Neither until you name one with `--promotion-tier 0`
choices.why: The tier orders replicas for a failover; the first instance is the writer from the start.

prompt: moto reports an Aurora cluster's `StorageType` as `gp2`. Why is that answer wrong, and not just unusual?

choices.text: gp2 is too slow for Aurora, which needs io2
choices.why: Aurora uses no EBS type at all, fast or slow.

choices.text: An Aurora volume is not an EBS disk
choices.why: Right. moto borrowed a field from its model of an ordinary instance.

choices.text: gp2 was retired, and moto should say gp3
choices.why: gp3 would be just as wrong; neither is Aurora storage.

choices.text: Aurora clusters report no storage type at all
choices.why: They do report one, `aurora` or `aurora-iopt1`, which is how the billing mode is shown.

prompt: Quitanda's first `create-db-cluster` named no storage size. What decides how much storage the cluster pays for?
hint: RDS bills what it allocated. What does Aurora bill?

choices.text: A default of 100 GiB, raised by autoscaling
choices.why: That is an RDS instance's model; Aurora has no allocation to start from.

choices.text: The size given to the first instance
choices.why: Instances carry no storage in Aurora; moto's `1` is a placeholder.

choices.text: The data it holds, billed once
choices.why: Right. The six copies are AWS's cost, not a line on the bill.

choices.text: Six times the data, for the six copies
choices.why: The copies are not billed; you pay for the data once.

prompt: Why does an Aurora failover to a replica need no data to be copied or replayed?
hint: Where does the replica read from?

choices.text: The replica reads the same shared volume the writer wrote
choices.why: Right. It only has to start accepting writes, and the cluster endpoint moves to it.

choices.text: Aurora replicas are synchronous, like a Multi-AZ standby
choices.why: They are not synchronous copies at all: they have no copy, they share the volume.

choices.text: The data is restored from the latest snapshot during failover
choices.why: Nothing is restored; a snapshot would take far longer than thirty seconds.

choices.text: Failover waits until the replica has replayed the log
choices.why: The storage nodes apply the log; the replica has nothing of its own to catch up.

prompt: A cluster runs a writer and no replica, because nothing reads from a replica. What does that cost on the day the writer fails, by AWS's documentation?
hint: Something has to run the engine against the volume.

choices.text: Nothing: the six copies in storage take over
choices.why: The copies hold data; they do not run an engine or accept connections.

choices.text: The data written since the last snapshot
choices.why: No data is lost: the volume survives the instance.

choices.text: A new instance has to start: under ten minutes by AWS's figure, instead of about thirty seconds
choices.why: Right. One replica, even an idle one, is what makes failover fast.

choices.text: The volume has to be restored into a new cluster
choices.why: The cluster and its volume stay; only an instance is missing.

prompt: Match each Aurora endpoint to the traffic Quitanda sends it.
hint: One of them is never for an application.

pairs.right: The analysts' heavy reports, on a replica of their own

prompt: By AWS's documentation, what is the largest number of instances an Aurora cluster can have, writer included?
A database needs 16 GiB of memory around the clock. What does the lesson's arithmetic say about running it on Serverless v2 instead of a `db.r7g.large`?
hint: 16 GiB is 8 ACUs at 0.25 an ACU-hour.

choices.text: About the same, since both are billed by the hour
choices.why: 8 ACUs cost 2.00 an hour against 0.43884; the unit is the same and the price is not.

choices.text: Cheaper, because serverless scales down when idle
choices.why: This database is never idle, so there is nothing to scale down.

choices.text: About 4.6 times the price: 1,460.00 a month against 320.35
choices.why: Right. Serverless wins when the load is mostly absent, not when it is constant.

choices.text: Impossible, because serverless stops at 8 ACUs
choices.why: The documented maximum is far higher, 256 ACUs on recent versions.

prompt: At 8 ACUs and 0.25 USD per ACU-hour, how many hours a month at full size can a cluster that pauses when idle run before it costs more than a `db.r7g.large` at 320.35 a month?
hint: Divide the monthly price by the hourly cost of 8 ACUs.

prompt: Why does the lesson put a minimum of 0 with auto-pause on the development cluster, and not on the shop's?
hint: What happens to the first connection after a pause?

choices.text: The first connection waits for it to wake
choices.why: Right. Seconds of waiting are fine for a developer and not for the morning's first customer.

choices.text: A paused cluster loses its data after 24 hours
choices.why: Storage stays, and is billed, while compute is paused.

choices.text: The shop's cluster is provisioned, which cannot pause
choices.why: The question is about which cluster should pause, and why.

choices.text: Auto-pause is only for MySQL
choices.why: This lesson's cluster is Aurora PostgreSQL and moto stored the setting.

prompt: One `db.r7g.large` and 500 GB. I/O-Optimized adds 96.34 a month for the instance and 119.00 for storage, and Standard charges 0.28 per million I/Os. Above how many million I/Os a month is I/O-Optimized cheaper? Round to the nearest whole number.
Quitanda adds a third `db.r7g.large` to its cluster. What happens to the break-even point between Standard and I/O-Optimized?

choices.text: It falls, since replicas add no storage
choices.why: No storage is added, and the instance premium still grows, so the line rises.

choices.text: It rises by about 344 million I/Os a month
choices.why: Right. 96.34 more of instance premium, divided by 0.28.

choices.text: It does not move; only storage sets it
choices.why: Instances and storage both carry a premium under I/O-Optimized.

choices.text: It disappears: three instances always favour I/O-Optimized
choices.why: More instances raise the fixed premium, which favours Standard until the I/O grows.

prompt: After switching to I/O-Optimized, the I/O line of Quitanda's bill is gone. What has the lesson warned that this hides?
hint: A missing index on Standard shows up as money.

choices.text: Storage growth, which is now free
choices.why: Storage is billed at 0.428 a GB-month, more than on Standard.

choices.text: The replicas, which are no longer billed
choices.why: Every instance is still billed, at a higher hourly price.

choices.text: A slow query, now unpriced
choices.why: Right. It is just as slow; only the invoice stopped saying so.

choices.text: Writes, which are now asynchronous
choices.why: The billing mode changes nothing about how storage is written.

prompt: Put the steps of building Quitanda's Aurora cluster in order.
hint: The cluster exists before any machine.
items: `create-db-cluster`, which makes the volume and the two endpoints
The first `create-db-instance`, which becomes the writer
A second instance in another zone, as a replica

prompt: A reporting database is used two hours each morning and idle the rest of the day; its I/O is small. Which Aurora set-up fits what the lesson priced?
hint: Two levers: how capacity is billed, and how I/O is billed.

choices.text: A provisioned `db.r7g.large` on I/O-Optimized
choices.why: It pays for 730 hours to use about 44, and a premium for I/O it barely does.

choices.text: Serverless v2 with auto-pause, on Standard storage
choices.why: Right. Far below the 160 hours where serverless stops winning, and too little I/O for I/O-Optimized to pay.

choices.text: Serverless v2 with a minimum equal to its maximum
choices.why: That is a provisioned instance billed at serverless prices, 4.6 times as much.

choices.text: Two provisioned instances, so the reports run on a replica
choices.why: Nothing else uses this database, so a replica only doubles the idle hours.

prompt: Which of these follow from Aurora's shared volume? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of what replicas no longer need.

choices.text: A replica adds no storage to the bill
choices.why: Yes; there is one volume.

choices.text: Replica lag is documented in milliseconds
choices.why: Yes; replicas read the same data and only refresh their memory.

choices.text: Failover to a replica copies no data
choices.why: Yes; the data is already where it can read it.

choices.text: A `DELETE` without a `WHERE` can be undone from a replica
choices.why: The replica reads the same volume, so it sees the delete at once; backups undo it.

choices.text: I/O stops being billed
choices.why: Only on I/O-Optimized, which is a billing choice and not a property of the volume.
